title: About us
text:
Chronologies was founded to meet the growing need for independent, informed advice on scientific dating. With over 25 years of experience in the field, we bring deep expertise in the application, interpretation, and integration of scientific dating methods across a wide range of archaeological contexts.






Our work has supported major research and heritage-led investigations across the United Kingdom and internationally. Notable projects include [Stonehenge], [Neolithic Orkney], and [Project Name 3] — demonstrating our ability to apply chronological tools to complex archaeological questions. These collaborations have contributed to refine our understanding of cultural change, environmental adaptation, and human mobility across different temporal and geographical contexts.


Further details on these and other collaborations can be found on our [Research] page.
We are also active contributors to the development of dating guidance and best practice. Our co-authored publications include nationally recognised frameworks and methodological reviews, helping to shape the standards by which dating evidence is commissioned, evaluated, and used. Key examples include Radiocarbon Dating & Chronological Modelling and Scientific Dating for Pleistocene Sites
Whether advising on sampling strategy, evaluating multi-method chronologies, or supporting publication and otreach, we are committed to delivering clear, context-aware, and scientifically robust input at every stage of the archaeological process.

Chronologies is a trusted provider of independent, expert advice on scientific dating for archaeological & heritage research. We work closely with academic institutions, heritage professionals, and commercial archaeologists to provide robust, contextually informed chronological frameworks.
Whether you require strategic guidance during project design or expert analysis of complex scientific dating results, we deliver tailored support grounded in current best practice and the latest scientific developments.
At Chronologies, we are committed to enhancing the reliability and interpretive power of archaeological chronologies. Let our expertise guide your next project with confidence and precision.

title: Chronologies Research
text:
The map below contains links to all our research.







How to use
The map provides a spatial overview of some of the sites & projects we have been fortunate to have worked on.

Basic Navigation: Use the + and - buttons (top left) to zoom in and out of the map Click and drag to pan around different geographic areas
Finding Sites: Markers indicate sites or project we have been involved with. Click on any marker for links to further information
Using the Archaeological Period Filters: The checkboxes on the right side of the map allow you to filter research sites and projects by archaeological period.
How to Filter by Period: Select periods of interest: Click the checkboxes next to the archaeological periods you wish to view. Multiple periods can be selected simultaneously to compare sites across different time periods.
View results: Sites and projects dating to your selected periods will remain visible on the map, while others will be hidden.
Clear filters: Uncheck boxes to remove periods from your view, or uncheck all boxes to return to the full dataset view.

title: Publications
text:
One of the most enduring rituals of ‘academic life’ is the dutiful compilation of publications—that familiar litany of books and journal articles for which one must claim responsibility. Presumably this exercise demonstrates scholarly credibility to colleagues.


While I no longer navigate the corridors of academic institutions, I haven’t entirely abandoned the habit of cataloguing my research output. The record below contains some highlights, for a longer list see Research Gate and Google Scholar.
During my time at English Heritage & Historic England, my research centered on understanding past human behaviors and environmental conditions through scientific analysis—particularly the application of radiocarbon dating and related chronometric techniques to archaeological contexts.
The work encompassed radiocarbon calibration, Bayesian statistical modeling of dates, taphonomic processes affecting organic preservation, stable isotope analysis, and the integration of multiple dating methods for robust chronological frameworks. I also explored broader questions of how environmental change influenced cultural transitions and settlement patterns in the archaeological record.
In my current role, my research output has naturally diminished compared to those more productive years. Nevertheless, my ongoing work as a scientific dating consultant continues to generate findings worthy of publication, and these contributions are gradually appearing in specialist journals & books.
Some recent publcations are detailed below
Greaney S, Hajdas I, Dee M, Marshall P. 2025. Beginning of the circle? Revised chronologies for Flagstones and Alington Avenue, Dorchester, Dorset. Antiquity, 99(405):655-671. doi:10.15184/aqy.2025.28



Grant, M. & Marshall, P. (eds) 2025 Scientific Dating of Pleistocene Sites: Guidelines for Best Practice. Historic England, London. availabe here
Bayliss, A, Brown, D, Dee, M, Marshall, P, & Wacker, L. 2024. Caveat emptor! - Wiggle-matching European wood samples (AD 46–AD 286), Radiocarbon, 66(3):580-596. doi:10.1017/RDC.2024.54
Marshall, P, Bayliss, A, Bronk Ramsey, C, Cook, G, & Reimer, P, 2024. Radiocarbon Dates from samples funded by English Heritage between 2010 and 2015, Historic England, Swindon. availabe here
